blogs.title: No Signature Required: The Fifth Circuit’s Textual Approach to “Certifying” Under La. R.S. 9:3550(G)(3)(a)
blogs.description: This post analyzes the court’s conclusion that the statute’s requirement of a statement “certifying” certain facts does not implicitly require a handwritten or electronic signature before cancellation is effective. It unpacks the court’s reliance on the statutory text and the absence of Louisiana authority imposing a signature requirement, distinguishes Benitez v. Elsayed, and considers how this reading interacts with corporate attestations and modern business practices. The post also explores the evidentiary and compliance implications for premium finance companies that issue unsigned, company-level certifications.

blogs.title: When Is Notice “Received” in the Digital Age? Machine Receipt and Automatic Cancellation Under Louisiana Premium Finance Law
blogs.description: Focusing on the meaning of “receipt” in La. R.S. 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i), this post examines the holding that delivery to the insurer’s web service—followed by automatic system cancellation—constitutes receipt. It assesses the Fifth Circuit’s reliance on Black’s Law Dictionary, the court’s embrace of electronic communications contemplated by the statute, and the operational details (APAC’s system calling GoAuto’s web service). The post flags practical issues for insurers and finance companies, including audit logs, system downtime, and how to prove machine receipt if challenged.

blogs.title: Strict Adherence, Modern Methods: Reconciling Eaglin, Britten, and Automated Cancellations
blogs.description: Louisiana courts have long demanded strict compliance for premium finance cancellations, with any defect rendering cancellation ineffective. This post explores how Williams v. GoAuto preserves that doctrine while declining to add requirements not in the statute (such as a pre-cancellation signature or human handling). It discusses whether the decision signals a shift from hyper-formalism to text-centered formalism that accounts for automation, and identifies where strictness remains most acute: proof of mailing, third-party notice, and the content of the finance company’s certification.

blogs.title: The District Court’s “Private Carrier” Theory That Wasn’t: A Curious Detour the Fifth Circuit Declined to Take
blogs.description: The district court justified compliance by analogizing an APAC employee to a “private carrier,” an imaginative reading that borrowed from railroad law. The Fifth Circuit affirmed on different grounds and declined to endorse that rationale. This post critiques the private-carrier theory against the statutory text (which separately references mail, private carrier, and electronic mail), explains why the appellate court’s avoidance matters, and offers guidance to trial courts and practitioners on avoiding tenuous analogies when the statute already squarely addresses electronic transmission.

blogs.title: Declining to Certify: Federal-State Judicial Dialogue and the Fifth Circuit’s Erie Prediction on Insurance Cancellations
blogs.description: Addressing the court’s refusal to certify interpretive questions to the Louisiana Supreme Court, this post reviews the Fifth Circuit’s certification standards and its reliance on Jefferson v. Lead Industries. It considers the pros and cons of an Erie prediction in a regulated insurance space, the potential for divergence if Louisiana appellate courts later take a different view, and strategic implications for litigants weighing state versus federal fora when unresolved issues in Louisiana’s premium finance statute are at stake.

blogs.title: Compliance Playbook After Williams: What Insurers and Premium Finance Companies Should Do Now
blogs.description: This practitioner-focused post distills concrete takeaways from the decision: ensuring the certification tracks La. R.S. 9:3550(G)(3)(a)(i)–(iv), maintaining reliable electronic transmission and receipt logs, aligning system timestamps with cancellation effective times, and documenting notices to interested third parties. It also explains why class action claims for misrepresentation and bad faith may fail if cancellation is effective, and identifies residual plaintiff avenues (e.g., defects in the 10-day notice, proof of mailing, or incomplete third-party notifications).
